clusters.title: Clock ticking for leap second: Why timekeeping could change forever
clusters.snippet: Timekeepers add a leap second occasionally to keep our clocks and the Earth's rotation in tune. That could now change.
also: Leap seconds face judgment day as time lords prepare to vote
clusters.text: Timekeepers add a leap second occasionally to keep our clocks and the Earth’s rotation in tune. That could now change. The world’s timekeepers are meeting on Thursday near Paris to decide whether to scrap the “leap second”, which could disconnect the clocks we use from the Earth’s rotation and realign timescales. The world’s clocks are designed on the idea that the Earth completes one rotation on its axis in exactly 24 hours. But it actually wobbles, making the time the Earth takes to rotate less exact. And over time, the Earth’s rotation is gradually slowing. To compensate for that, since 1972, timekeepers have added a leap second every few years – the last one was added in 2016 – to keep clocks and Earth’s rotation in synchronisation. But pressure has been mounting to scrap the leap second since it complicates matters for financial markets and data centres, which rely on precise timing down to milliseconds. So what is a leap second? Could it be scrapped? And how might it change our understanding of time? Clocks work based on Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the global standard that has been based on high-precision atomic clocks for more than seven decades. Atomic clocks mark time by observing the vibration of atoms. But the Earth’s rotation works independently of atomic clocks. A leap second is a second added periodically to UTC to make it synchronise with the Earth’s rotation. The first leap second was added to world clocks in 1972. There have been 27 leap seconds added so far with the previous leap second being added on December 31, 2016. No further leap seconds have been added since. According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), a nonregulatory federal agency of the United States Department of Commerce, leap seconds occur at the end of December or the end of June. The NIST also cites differences between the precision of the atomic second and the Earth’s rotation to explain the need for a leap second. “The speed of the Earth’s rotation is not constant. …. This gradual decrease in the rotational rate is causing the duration of the mean solar second to gradually increase with respect to the atomic second,” the NIST added. While leap seconds close the discrepancy between the Earth’s rotation and UTC, their addition has posed challenges for technology companies, financial markets and other businesses that depend on precise timings.

clusters.text: The $50 Xbox Nano Controller is five inches long and weighs 3.5 ounces. Xbox has unveiled its latest gamepad , which it says is the smallest controller in its lineup. The Xbox Nano Controller is just over five inches long and weighs 3.5 ounces. It offers the standard Xbox controller layout in a more compact format. Xbox says the controller, which has a rechargeable battery, could be useful for younger players and others with smaller hands. It has an action button you can program via the Xbox Accessories app to, for instance, take screenshots or gameplay videos. There's Bluetooth support so, along with Xbox consoles and PCs, the Nano Controller is compatible with iOS and Android devices as well as certain smart TVs. Samsung is bundling the controller and two months of Game Pass Ultimate access for new subscribers with select TV purchases in the US during the holiday season. A similar offer is in the works for Meta Quest headsets. It's worth bearing in mind that Xbox is enabling time limits on cloud gaming as of next month. You'll only be able to stream cloud games on a TV, Quest or other device for 15 hours with Game Pass Ultimate unless you buy time credits. The Nano Controller reminds me of the more portable gamepads that 8BitDo makes, though it's not quite as teeny as that brand's Micro controller . I'm interested in trying it to find out how the Nano's triggers feel. I play games on my phone using the BackBone Pro and OhSnap's MCON and while I broadly like both, I find the triggers on those controllers finicky. Pre-orders for the Xbox Nano Controller are now open. The peripheral costs $50 and it'll ship in the US on November 4. It'll be available in 35 other countries next month and it will hit other markets down the line.

clusters.title: CMPDIL signs MoU with HLL Lifecare to set up ‘AMRIT Pharmacy’ at Ranchi headquarters
also: CMPDIL Signs MoU with HLL Lifecare for AMRIT Pharmacy in Ranchi
clusters.text: Ranchi, Oct 14: Central Mine Planning & Design Institute Limited (CMPDIL), a Mini-Ratna company and subsidiary of Coal India Limited, has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with HLL Lifecare Limited, a Government of India enterprise, to set up, operate and maintain an ‘AMRIT Pharmacy’ at its headquarters in Ranchi. The initiative aims to provide affordable medicines and allied healthcare products to CMPDIL employees, their dependents and the general public. The MoU was signed by Sanjay Kadambar, General Manager (HR), on behalf of CMPDIL, and Sanjay Kumar Gupta, Deputy General Manager and Regional Manager (Retail Business Division), on behalf of HLL Lifecare Limited. The signing took place in the presence of Chaudhari Shivraj Singh, CMD, CMPDI, and other dignitaries. The pharmacy will supply medicines, surgical items, implants and other related healthcare products within the CMPDIL premises, ensuring convenient access to essential healthcare products at affordable prices. The establishment of the AMRIT Pharmacy reflects CMPDIL’s commitment to employee welfare and social responsibility. The initiative is expected to improve healthcare convenience for employees and their families while extending its benefits to the wider community.
